subject: beetle
reasoning:
I'm planning out a stag beetle model at roughly 5cm body length facing forward, with a head, pronotum, elytra, six jointed legs, large mandible-like antlers, and antennae with clubs, structuring the skeleton with a root body joint and child joints for each part.

For legs, I'm deciding to skip chain helpers and instead build joints connected by rods or capsules, since that gives more direct control over hip-knee-foot segments. I'm also settling on a dark brown-black palette for the body and elytra, with a glossy mandible color, and considering using a grain paint texture along the elytra for a mottled shell effect.

Now I'm working out the coordinate layout—body facing +Z, legs touching the floor at y=0, and placing joints for the root body, head, and mandibles as children in a hierarchy, using the "jaw" role for the mandible hinges so they can be posed open like pincers.

For the mandibles, I'm sketching them as curved, antler-like capsule sweeps built along catmull-rom paths going up and outward. For the legs, I'm setting up mirrored joint chains (hip, knee, ankle, foot) for each of the three leg pairs on both sides, connecting them with capsules between joint frames, and planning small cone shapes for claws at the foot tips.

Now I'm working out how to name and structure these joints so they satisfy naming rules while keeping the leg hierarchy clean, then turning to the elytra shell, which I want to build as a swept ellipse-section path running along the body's spine with a radius function controlling width and height at each point.

Using loft stations instead, defining width/height tapers from the shoulder dome down to a pointed tail, bound to the body joint for weighting, then splitting into left and right halves offset along x to leave a midline groove.

I'm also sketching the pronotum shield as another loft that overlaps the front of the elytra, tapering from a narrow head-side edge to a wider dome before blending into the thorax.

For the head, I'm shaping a slightly flattened, elongated sphere scaled unevenly to look less spherical, attaching it at the head joint. I'm adding glossy near-black eye spheres on each side of the head, then building the stag beetle's oversized mandibles as curved sweeps from base joints that arc upward and forward toward a tapered tip, using control points in local space.

I'm giving each mandible a gradual radius taper from thick base to thin point, plus a small spike jutting off the inner edge as an extra tooth, explicitly binding the sweep to the mandible joint so it follows the joint's pose correctly. For the antennae, I'm planning simple tapered sweeps topped with a small clustered club shape.

Now I'm working through leg placement for all three pairs, defining hip, knee, ankle, and foot joints with coordinates that angle outward and downward, tapering the capsule radii from thick femur to thin tarsus so the feet land near ground level. I'm settling on a consistent naming scheme like hipFL, kneeFL, ankleFL across the front, middle, and hind leg pairs on each side.

I'm building the mandibles with a curved sweep tapering toward the tip, adding a small inward-pointing tooth spike partway along, and setting up joints so they could be posed open if desired, though I'm leaning toward skipping explicit posing to keep the rest geometry simple.

I'm also laying out the head sphere, eyes, and a segmented antenna sweep ending in a club shape, then moving to loft the thorax and elytra with layered stations that taper toward the tail, using a mottled brown paint grain for the wing cases that meet cleanly along the body's midline. Finally I'm defining color values for body, legs, mandibles, eyes, and claws, and adding a small claw spike at each foot joint pointing downward into the ground.

Working through the leg chains now — each pair gets a hip-knee-ankle-foot joint sequence built as a chain, with tapered capsule segments between them and a claw spike at the tip — while double-checking that joint positions, radii, and the floor contact height all stay proportionate to the model's overall scale before assembling everything under the root body joint.
